title: When Teams Are Not Really Teams
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the reflex to call any working group a team, arguing that many so-called teams are actually loose collections of independent performers who share a label but not interdependent goals. It explains why full-group meetings for these collectives tend to be dull and disengaging, since the shared updates rarely matter to everyone in the room. Rather than manufacturing a false sense of shared purpose, the piece recommends replacing large group meetings with rotating three-way conversations, pairing the leader with two members at a time so peers learn from and about each other's work. The underlying message is that leaders should adapt their structure to reality instead of forcing team dynamics onto a group that isn't structurally a team.
points: Many groups are labeled teams even though members work independently with no shared outcomes.
Full-group meetings for these collectives tend to be boring and disengaging for most attendees.
By definition, a real team requires interdependent members with a common purpose and shared outcomes.
Manufacturing a false shared goal to force team behavior usually backfires.
Rotating three-way meetings, pairing the leader with two members at a time, build peer relationships instead.
quotes: Not surprisingly, these meetings are a death march and so boring that anyone not speaking checks out and disengages.
The group is a loose collection of individual performers and will not operate as a team no matter what strategy the leader employs.
By definition, a team is comprised of highly interdependent members with a common purpose and a shared set of outcomes.
Giving the group a false purpose or common goal will often compound the problem.
Asking each of the parties to apply their smarts and sense-making to the other creates a robust learning conversation that becomes invaluable over time.
Sometimes unity exists in the conversation and not in a common goal.
